column3: Near-verbatim counterpart: those with Him neither refuse worship nor grow weary.
Adds the uncut reward for faith and righteous work; later reward cards are largely redundant.
Confirms the return by gathering to Allah, but adds little beyond that route.
Closest parallel: those near their Lord reject neither worship nor prostration, not self-exaltation.
Only shares the broader nearby-channel setting; its speech rule does not clarify the focus.
Joins total gathering with angels and a scrutiny of alleged worship directed to them.
Places the Messiah's own call to worship Allah against identifying him with Allah.
Immediate predecessor: bounds claims about the Messiah and affirms Allah's oneness.
Immediate continuation supplies the corresponding reward and punishment for service or proud refusal.
Excludes taking angels or prophets as lords, sharpening the focus's servant status for both.
Adds the delighted outcome for believers who do righteous work; it repeats the reward side.
The contrast-tagged record motif is boundary evidence, not support for the focus reading.
Again contests the Messiah's identification with Allah by stressing divine sovereignty over him.
Nearby channel membership alone supplies no usable connection to worship, pride, or gathering.
Shows withdrawal from rival worship toward Allah alone, a secondary exclusive-worship parallel.
Supplies the title of the near ones, but no service or refusal relation.
Adds just multiplication and great reward, supporting the recompense side after the direct continuation.
Its rejected contrast reading cannot positively support the focus's pride-and-service pattern.
Only repeats the near ones as witnesses, without clarifying their servant posture.
Adds righteous servants as inheritors, extending the positive servant outcome.
Reinforces dispersal followed by gathering to Him, though the gathering route is already well covered.
Names the Messiah among the near ones, directly qualifying proximity without divinization.
Provides only broad immediate-pericope context about divided belief.
Pairs worship of Allah alone with warning of painful punishment, but less specifically than the focus.
The near ones drinking adds only a narrow proximity association.
Combines worship without partners with rejection of boastful self-exaltation and concrete social conduct.
Keeps worshippers and their objects together, supporting a relational rather than isolated view of worship.
Links total divine ownership and return to Him, a secondary sovereignty-and-return frame.
Adds that righteous action prepares one's own outcome, extending the consequence side.
Maintains worship directed exclusively to Allah across changing places; a secondary servant parallel.
Adds the angels' ascent to Him, informing their dependent relation without naming worship.
Nearby condemnation supports the adverse outcome, but not the focus's specific refusal formulation.
Gathers wrongdoers with their associates and what they worship, tightly joining judgment and worship relations.
A grateful servant offers a positive exemplar but no specific proximity, pride, or gathering link.
Its disobedient speech pattern is too indirect despite the surah-level association.
Connects arrogant speech about Allah with humiliating punishment, extending the consequence of self-exaltation.
Angelic selection as messengers does not itself clarify their servant posture.
Identifies worshippers as the audience of the preceding servant-inheritance statement, but repeats that line.
A coercive human gathering is only a secondary, contrary gathering image.
Tests rejection even amid overwhelming angelic and gathered evidence; related but not a service parallel.
Immediate reward for undivided faith adds the positive side, though 4:173 is more direct.
Explicitly joins groundless self-exaltation with denying return to Allah.
Reopens the false claim about the Messiah as son, but repeats the stronger nearby correction.
The commanded prostration and covenant are a distant antecedent to refusal and pride.
States a unified worship orientation for jinn and humankind, broadening the focus's servant frame.
Universalizes arrival before the Merciful in the condition of a servant.
Adds recompense from divine bounty for believers' deeds, repeating the reward side.
Reaffirms that the Lord gathers all with wisdom and knowledge, though gathering is already established.
Iblis's refusal to be among prostrators supplies a contrasting refusal posture.
Immediate background of excessive demand and calf-taking is only indirect context.
Nonhuman gathering gives a distant forced-assembly image, not the focus's accountability relation.
Contrasts rival attachments with Allah's sole power at punishment, supporting undivided worship and accountability.
Channel membership alone does not connect this exemption for the powerless to the focus.
Pride in the earth fails to escape the divine outcome, directly extending self-exaltation's futility.
Defines a recipient of mercy and knowledge first as a servant, qualifying granted status as dependent.
Links worship and endurance in it to the Lord of all realms and rejects any equal.
The great sign has no usable focus link; the V12 association is too tangential.
Scenes the weak and self-exalting standing before their Lord, adding accountability for social pride.
Immediate context supplies hardened rejection, but no distinct service or gathering connection.
The legal travel rule ends with gathering to Him but contributes little beyond that repeated route.
Contrasts faithful submission to Allah's command with self-directed refusal of it.
Prayer concession and channel membership do not clarify the focus.
Shows self-exalting people rejecting what others affirm, a social form of proud refusal.
Places a servant at prayer under obstruction, preserving the voluntary-service versus coercion tension.
This immediate accusation against Mary adds no distinct connection to the focus reading.
Total gathering exposes claimed partners through direct questioning, tightly linking judgment and association.
The servant analogy offers a limited capacity contrast, but not the focus's worship or pride structure.
Angels descend only by their Lord's command, a limited secondary sign of dependence.
Depicts the compelled gathering of criminals, reinforcing the adverse gathering side.
An impending portion of what is sought has no usable service, pride, or gathering relation.
Immediate Christ-centered context matters, but the uncertainty about the killing claim is not the focus's issue.
Angels prostrate while Iblis refuses and grows proud, a sharp counter-pattern to the focus.
Divine command and the promise offer only a broad sovereignty frame.
Connects the absence of self-exaltation with a distinct social posture, but indirectly.
Calls to worship Allah and reverence Him, a clear but already redundant exclusive-worship parallel.
Combines response to Allah's call with eventual gathering to Him, linking obedience and return.
Immediate continuation locates the Messiah's raising in Allah's act and authority.
Servants' varying provision does not materially clarify service, pride, or gathering.
Gathering confronts alleged partners, then separates them as the alleged worship relation is denied.
Righteous servants and provision are too distant from the focus despite the branch resonance.
Makes self-exaltation a response to the assertion of Allah's sole divinity, though earlier cards cover it more fully.
The assumption of being beyond power is only a general pride-and-accountability analogue.
Immediate Christ context adds future witnessing, but not the focus's servant formulation.
Divine witness marks the claimed recipients of worship as unaware, adding a distinct relational denial.
Scattered people imagery alone has no clear route to the focus's service or judgment structure.
Repeats the uncut-reward formula already supplied more directly by 41:8.
Naming Zakariyya as a servant supplies only a generic servant association.
Opposition to the messenger and failed deeds is not a specific pride or worship parallel.
Ends with gathering to Him but is otherwise a redundant ritual-time context.
Contrasts turning to the Lord in distress with later setting up rivals, extending unstable worship allegiance.
Forbids social diminishment and superiority claims, a tail-audit ethical check on self-exaltation.
Maintains non-overlap in worship roles, a focused exclusive-worship boundary already supported elsewhere.
Immediate continuation adds faith, holding fast, mercy, and a path to Him as the positive trajectory.
Adds an ordered gathering of deniers for questioning, but repeats the judgment route.
Inheritance allocations do not add to the focus interpretation.
Frames messengers as human recipients of favor among Allah's servants, limiting elevated status.
Pilgrimage procedure and warning lack a usable focus connection.
Shows pride as turning people from signs and reversing their route choices, extending proud refusal.
The combat command has no material relation to the focus reading.
Limits authority over Allah's servants to those who follow a false route, adding an allegiance boundary.
Counters sonship claims by placing all in the heavens and earth in obedient relation to Allah.
Joins angelic witness to Allah's sole divinity, a supporting monotheism frame.
Places the Messiah's created comparison with Adam against exceptional-divine status.
Calls for worship of Allah alone and rejection of taking one another as lords.
Denies that a human given scripture and prophethood could demand worship for himself.
Directly states the certain gathering on the Day of Resurrection.
Immediate continuation offers the divine proof and light after the focus's service-and-gathering warning.
Challenges claims of special divine sonship by retaining shared human accountability.
Rejects a triadic claim about Allah, reinforcing the focus's anti-exaltation boundary.
Presents the Messiah and his mother as recipients of provision, limiting their status.
Has Allah question the Messiah about whether he directed worship to himself and his mother.
Records the Messiah's own command to worship Allah, his Lord and theirs.
Keeps forgiveness and punishment under Allah's authority over His servants.
States the certain gathering to the Day of Resurrection under divine mercy.
Names Allah as creator and commands worship of Him, with guardianship over all things.
Gathers jinn and humankind and exposes their mutually implicated associations.
Supplies the angelic prostration command and Iblis's refusal before the fuller pride account.
Calls alleged deities servants like their callers, undercutting rival worship.
Explicitly names taking religious authorities and the Messiah as lords against worship of one God.
Challenges worship of intercessory claimants who lack independent authority.
Reasserts exclusive worship of Allah at the boundary between belief and rejection.
Forbids calling on what neither benefits nor harms besides Allah.
States that judgment belongs to Allah and commands worship of Him alone.
Generalizes the command to worship Allah and avoid false authorities across communities.
Includes angels among those prostrating to Allah without self-exaltation.
Shows the angels fearing their Lord above them and doing what they are commanded.
Rejects multiple gods and directs reverent fear to Allah alone.
Portrays those invoked as themselves seeking nearness to their Lord.
Rejects childship, partnership, and any need for a protector in divine rule.
Links meeting the Lord to righteous work and worship without association.
The Messiah identifies himself first as Allah's servant and recipient of scripture.
Places worship of Allah within the Messiah narrative as the straight path.
Combines Allah's sole divinity with the direct command to worship Him.
Replays the angelic prostration and Iblis's refusal in a second narrative setting.
Commands persistence in prayer, extending enduring service rather than refusal.
Completes 21:19 with unceasing glorification by those who do not slacken.
Makes worship of Allah alone the common message of every messenger.
Calls the angels honored servants, directly qualifying their elevated proximity.
Warns any angel who claimed divinity besides Allah with recompense for wrongdoing.
Includes angels and many creatures in universal prostration, with an adverse judgment side.
Rejects divine sonship and multiple gods by affirming undivided divine sovereignty.
Pairs purposive creation with the return to Allah.
Contrasts worship of what cannot benefit or harm with allegiance against the Lord.
Defines servants of the Merciful through humility, a direct counter-posture to self-exaltation.
Sets an upright, unaltered orientation for religion against divided commitments.
Identifies associating partners with Allah as grave wrongdoing.
Describes believers prostrating when reminded and not growing proud.
Denies independent divine authority to those invoked besides Allah.
States that invoked beings cannot hear and would deny their worship on the Day of Resurrection.
Depicts all being brought together before Allah after a single cry.
Forbids worship of Satan and frames it as a clear opposing allegiance.
Commands worship of Allah as the straight path immediately after that prohibition.
Affirms the unity of the deity, a compressed monotheism support.
Commands worship of Allah as Lord over the forebears and all worlds.
Names Iblis's self-exaltation in the angelic prostration episode.
Commands sincere religion and worship directed to Allah.
Rejects intermediary worship claims made as routes to nearness to Allah.
Commands worship of Allah with religion made exclusively His.
Distinguishes those who avoid false authorities and turn back to Allah.
Records aversion when Allah alone is mentioned and preference for others besides Him.
Commands worship of Allah with religion sincerely His despite disbelievers' resistance.
Forbids prostration to celestial signs and commands prostration to their Creator.
Near-verbatim parallel: those with the Lord are not too proud for worship and glorify Him.
Defines the Messiah as a servant upon whom Allah bestowed favor.
Has the Messiah call to worship Allah as his Lord and theirs.
States that Allah gives life, causes death, and gathers all for the Day of Resurrection.
Combines prostration and worship in the closing command.
Places the Messiah explicitly in the role of messenger to Israel.
Names the Day of Gathering and its divergent outcomes.
Shows angels who do not disobey Allah and carry out what they are commanded.
Reserves places of worship for Allah and forbids invoking anyone with Him.
Names Allah's servant standing to call upon Him amid a crowding response.
Places angels and the Spirit in ordered standing under restricted speech.
Closes the prayer-obstruction passage with prostration and drawing near.
Commands worship of Allah with religion made sincere and exclusive to Him.
Affirms Allah's absolute oneness.
Affirms Allah's self-sufficiency against any dependent divine relation.
Rejects begetting and being begotten, directly opposing sonship claims.
Rejects any equivalence to Allah.
